claim: T cells use their T cell receptors (TCRs) to discriminate between lower-affinity self and higher-affinity non-self peptides presented on major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) antigens.
source: T cells use their T cell receptors (TCRs) to discriminate between lower-affinity self and higher-affinity non-self peptides presented on major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) antigens.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about T cell biology that is widely accepted in the field.

claim: The discriminatory power of the TCR is widely believed to be near-perfect.
source: Although the discriminatory power of the TCR is widely believed to be near-perfect, technical difficulties have hampered efforts to precisely quantify it.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies in the introduction.

claim: Technical difficulties have hampered efforts to precisely quantify TCR discriminatory power.
source: Although the discriminatory power of the TCR is widely believed to be near-perfect, technical difficulties have hampered efforts to precisely quantify it.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the current study and is supported by discussion of measurement challenges in the introduction.

claim: Primary human T cells can respond to pMHC with affinities as low as KD ∼ 1 mM.
source: We find that TCR discrimination, although enhanced compared with conventional cell-surface receptors, is imperfect: primary human T cells can respond to pMHC with affinities as low as KD ∼ 1 mM.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TCR discrimination is enhanced compared with conventional cell-surface receptors but is imperfect.
source: We find that TCR discrimination, although enhanced compared with conventional cell-surface receptors, is imperfect: primary human T cells can respond to pMHC with affinities as low as KD ∼ 1 mM.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data comparing TCR discrimination to other receptors (Figure 6).

claim: The kinetic proofreading mechanism fits the experimental data on TCR discrimination.
source: The kinetic proofreading mechanism fit our data, providing the first estimates of both the time delay (2.8 s) and number of biochemical steps (2.67) that are consistent with the extraordinary sensitivity of antigen recognition.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The kinetic proofreading time delay is 2.8 seconds.
source: The kinetic proofreading mechanism fit our data, providing the first estimates of both the time delay (2.8 s) and number of biochemical steps (2.67) that are consistent with the extraordinary sensitivity of antigen recognition.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the kinetic proofreading model to experimental data.

claim: The number of biochemical steps in kinetic proofreading is 2.67.
source: The kinetic proofreading mechanism fit our data, providing the first estimates of both the time delay (2.8 s) and number of biochemical steps (2.67) that are consistent with the extraordinary sensitivity of antigen recognition.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the kinetic proofreading model to experimental data.

claim: Self pMHC frequently induce autoimmune diseases.
source: Our findings explain why self pMHC frequently induce autoimmune diseases and anti-tumour responses, and suggest ways to modify TCR discrimination.
evidence: This is presented as an implication of the findings and is consistent with clinical observations.

claim: Self pMHC frequently induce anti-tumour responses.
source: Our findings explain why self pMHC frequently induce autoimmune diseases and anti-tumour responses, and suggest ways to modify TCR discrimination.
evidence: This is presented as an implication of the findings and is consistent with clinical observations.

claim: The strength of discrimination is widely believed to be near-perfect for the TCR.
source: Although the strength of discrimination is widely believed to be near-perfect for the TCR (Francois et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2014; Dushek and van der Merwe, 2014; Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014; Hong et al., 2018; Fernandes et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019; Ganti et al., 2020), systematic measurements to quantify it have not been performed.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Systematic measurements to quantify TCR discrimination have not been performed.
source: Although the strength of discrimination is widely believed to be near-perfect for the TCR (Francois et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2014; Dushek and van der Merwe, 2014; Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014; Hong et al., 2018; Fernandes et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019; Ganti et al., 2020), systematic measurements to quantify it have not been performed.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: Early influential studies using three murine TCRs suggested a sharp affinity threshold for T cell activation.
source: Early influential studies using three murine TCRs suggested a sharp affinity threshold for T cell activation (Hogquist et al., 1995; Alam et al., 1996; Alam et al., 1999; Kersh and Allen, 1996; Kersh et al., 1998b; Lyons et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Subtle changes to cognate peptides produced modest three- to fivefold decreases in affinity that abolished T cell responses even when increasing peptide concentration by as much as 100,000-fold.
source: Using T cells from the OT-I, 3.L2, and 2B4 transgenic TCR mice, it was shown that subtle changes to their cognate peptides, which apparently produced modest three- to fivefold decreases in affinity, abolished T cell responses even when increasing the peptide concentration by as much as 100,000-fold (Hogquist et al., 1995; Alam et al., 1996; Alam et al., 1999; Kersh and Allen, 1996; Kersh et al., 1998b; Lyons et al., 1996; Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Near-perfect discrimination based on affinity can be explained by a kinetic proofreading mechanism.
source: Although this near-perfect discrimination based on affinity could be explained by a kinetic proofreading (KP) mechanism (McKeithan, 1995), it could not also account for the ability of T cells to respond to few pMHC ligands (high sensitivity; Huang et al., 2013; Siller-Farfán and Dushek, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McKeithan, 1995.

claim: The kinetic proofreading mechanism could not account for the ability of T cells to respond to few pMHC ligands (high sensitivity).
source: Although this near-perfect discrimination based on affinity could be explained by a kinetic proofreading (KP) mechanism (McKeithan, 1995), it could not also account for the ability of T cells to respond to few pMHC ligands (high sensitivity; Huang et al., 2013; Siller-Farfán and Dushek, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: There has been a focus on identifying mechanisms that can simultaneously explain near-perfect discrimination and high sensitivity.
source: Consequently, there has been a focus on identifying mechanisms that can simultaneously explain near-perfect discrimination and high sensitivity (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Francois et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2014; Dushek and van der Merwe, 2014; Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014; Hong et al., 2018; Fernandes et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019; Ganti et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Near-perfect discrimination is inconsistent with evidence that T cells can respond to lower-affinity self-antigens.
source: However, near-perfect discrimination is inconsistent with evidence that T cells can respond to lower-affinity self-antigens (Yin et al., 2012; Bridgeman et al., 2012), and moreover, that T cell-mediated autoimmunity is associated with increased expression of self-antigens (Korem Kohanim et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: T cell-mediated autoimmunity is associated with increased expression of self-antigens.
source: However, near-perfect discrimination is inconsistent with evidence that T cells can respond to lower-affinity self-antigens (Yin et al., 2012; Bridgeman et al., 2012), and moreover, that T cell-mediated autoimmunity is associated with increased expression of self-antigens (Korem Kohanim et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: There is a discrepancy between the current notion of near-perfect TCR discrimination and data on the role of T cell recognition of self-pMHC in human disease.
source: There is thus a discrepancy between the current notion of near-perfect TCR discrimination and data on the role of T cell recognition of self-pMHC in human disease.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inconsistencies described in the preceding sentences.

claim: A key challenge in assessing discrimination is the accurate measurements of very weak TCR/pMHC affinities, with KD ranging from 1 to >100 μM.
source: A key challenge in assessing discrimination is the accurate measurements of very weak TCR/pMHC affinities, with KD ranging from 1 to >100 μM (van der Merwe and Davis, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) is a highly sensitive method for analysing molecular interactions.
source: A highly sensitive method for analysing molecular interactions is surface plasmon resonance (SPR), but even with this method, accurate measurements are difficult to make, especially at 37°C.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SPR as a technique.

claim: Accurate measurements of weak TCR/pMHC interactions are difficult to make with SPR, especially at 37°C.
source: A highly sensitive method for analysing molecular interactions is surface plasmon resonance (SPR), but even with this method, accurate measurements are difficult to make, especially at 37°C.
evidence: This is stated as a technical challenge and is supported by discussion of specific examples.

claim: OT-I measurements at 37°C showed high-affinity biphasic binding, which has not been observed for other TCRs.
source: In the case of OT-I, for example, measurements were performed at 37°C but high-affinity biphasic binding was observed (Alam et al., 1999), which has not been observed for other TCRs and may represent protein aggregates that often form at the high concentrations necessary for making these measurements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Alam et al., 1999 and comparison to other TCRs.

claim: The reported small threefold change in affinity between the activating OVA and non-activating E1 ligands may be a consequence of multivalent interactions.
source: It follows that the reported small threefold change in affinity between the activating OVA and non-activating E1 ligands (Alam et al., 1999) may be a consequence of multivalent interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of biphasic binding.

claim: More recent studies found the expected low-affinity monophasic binding for OT-I/OVA.
source: Indeed, more recent studies found the expected low-affinity monophasic binding for OT-I/OVA (Stepanek et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015) and no detectable binding for OT-I/E1 (Stepanek et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to more recent studies.

claim: No detectable binding was found for OT-I/E1 in more recent studies.
source: Indeed, more recent studies found the expected low-affinity monophasic binding for OT-I/OVA (Stepanek et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015) and no detectable binding for OT-I/E1 (Stepanek et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stepanek et al., 2014.

claim: E1 may not activate T cells not because of near-perfect discrimination but simply because it does not bind the TCR.
source: This raises the possibility that E1 does not activate T cells not because of near-perfect discrimination but simply because it does not bind the TCR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding of no detectable binding for OT-I/E1.

claim: A new SPR protocol can accurately determine ultra-low TCR/pMHC affinities at 37°C into the KD ∼1 mM regime.
source: Here, we introduce a new SPR protocol that can accurately determine ultra-low TCR/pMHC affinities at 37°C into the KD ∼1 mM regime.
evidence: This is a methodological contribution of the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: T cell responses were gradually lost as the affinity was decreased without a sharp affinity threshold.
source: We found that T cell responses were gradually lost as the affinity was decreased without a sharp affinity threshold and remarkably responses were detected to ultra-low-affinity pMHCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Responses were detected to ultra-low-affinity pMHCs.
source: We found that T cell responses were gradually lost as the affinity was decreased without a sharp affinity threshold and remarkably responses were detected to ultra-low-affinity pMHCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The discriminatory power of the T cell receptor is imperfect yet remains above the baseline produced by other conventional surface receptors.
source: By introducing a quantitative measure of discrimination, we are able to not only analyse our data but also analyse the published literature finding that the discriminatory power of the T cell receptor is imperfect yet remains above the baseline produced by other conventional surface receptors.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by analysis of experimental data and literature (Figures 3 and 6).

claim: The standard SPR protocol is based on injecting the TCR at increasing concentrations over a pMHC-coated surface.
source: The standard SPR protocol is based on injecting the TCR at increasing concentrations over a pMHC-coated surface (Figure 1A and B) with the resulting steady-state binding response plotted over the TCR concentration (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the standard SPR method and references Figure 1.

claim: KD is the TCR concentration where binding is half the Bmax.
source: This curve is fitted by a two-parameter Hill function to determine Bmax (the maximum response when all pMHCs are bound by TCR) and the KD, which is the TCR concentration where binding is half the Bmax.
evidence: This is a standard definition in binding kinetics.

claim: An accurate determination of KD requires an accurate determination of Bmax.
source: Therefore, an accurate determination of KD requires an accurate determination of Bmax.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the relationship between KD and Bmax.

claim: The 1G4 TCR binding to its cognate NY-ESO-1 peptide produces KD ≈ 7 μM.
source: In the case of the 1G4 TCR binding to its cognate NY-ESO-1 peptide, this protocol produces KD ≈ 7 μM (Figure 1A–C, left column).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 1.

claim: The binding response curves do not saturate for lower-affinity pMHCs.
source: However, the binding response curves do not saturate for lower-affinity pMHCs (Figure 1A–C, right column).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The fitted Bmax and therefore the fitted KD may not be accurate for lower-affinity pMHCs.
source: Because of this, the fitted Bmax and therefore the fitted KD may not be accurate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that binding curves do not saturate.

claim: Saturating the binding curves by increasing the TCR concentration is limited by the tendency of soluble recombinant proteins to accumulate aggregates at high concentrations.
source: Saturating the binding curves by increasing the TCR concentration is limited by the tendency of soluble recombinant proteins, including the TCR, to accumulate aggregates at high concentrations, which precludes accurate SPR measurements.
evidence: This is a known technical limitation in protein biochemistry.

claim: W6/32 is a conformation-sensitive, pan-HLA-A/B/C antibody that only binds correctly folded pMHC.
source: To determine Bmax when saturating pMHC with TCR was not feasible (i.e. for lower-affinity interactions), we generated a standard curve using the conformation-sensitive, pan-HLA-A/B/C antibody (W6/32) that only binds correctly folded pMHC (Brodskys and Parham, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brodskys and Parham, 1982.

claim: A linear relationship was observed between fitted Bmax from higher-affinity interactions and maximum W6/32 binding.
source: By injecting the W6/32 antibody at the end of each experiment (Figure 1B, black line), we were able to plot the fitted Bmax from higher-affinity interactions (where binding saturated) over the maximum W6/32 binding (Figure 1D). We observed a linear relationship even when including different TCRs binding different pMHC across multiple protein preparations immobilised at different levels.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: W6/32 and the TCR recognise the same correctly folded active pMHC population.
source: Together, this strongly suggested that W6/32 and the TCR recognise the same correctly folded active pMHC population and justified the use of the standard curve to estimate Bmax.
evidence: This is an inference based on the linear relationship observed between W6/32 binding and TCR Bmax.

claim: The immobilisation level cannot be used to estimate Bmax because only a fraction of the pMHC immobilised is correctly folded and this fraction varies between protein preparations.
source: While the level of W6/32 binding and Bmax is approximately proportional to the pMHC immobilisation level (see data for the NYE 9V pMHC in Figure 1D), the immobilisation level cannot be used to estimate Bmax because only a fraction of the pMHC immobilised is correctly folded and this fraction varies between protein preparations.
evidence: This is an explanation for why W6/32 binding is used instead of immobilisation level.

claim: Both the standard method (Bmax fitted) and the new method (Bmax constrained) produced similar KD values for higher affinities.
source: We next fitted KD values for 132 interactions using the standard method where Bmax is fitted and the new method where Bmax is constrained to the value obtained using the standard curve (Figure 1E). In the new method, the only fitted parameter is KD. Both methods produced similar KD values for higher affinities, validating the method (e.g. Figure 1C, left).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Large (100-fold) discrepancies appeared for lower-affinity interactions, with the fitted Bmax method consistently underestimating the KD.
source: In contrast, large (100-fold) discrepancies appeared for lower-affinity interactions, with the fitted Bmax method consistently underestimating the KD.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from comparing the two methods.

claim: For the fitted Bmax method, different combinations of Bmax and KD can provide a fit of similar quality so that the fitted KD can exhibit large variations for the same interaction.
source: This suggested that for the fitted Bmax method different combinations of Bmax and KD can provide a fit of similar quality so that the fitted KD can exhibit large variations for the same interaction (also known as 'over-fitting').
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of large discrepancies despite similar fit quality.

claim: The standard method has lower precision for low-affinity interactions as a result of over-fitting.
source: We explored this by comparing the precision of both methods using the coefficient of variance (CV) of multiple measurements of the same TCR/pMHC combination. We found a similar CV for higher-affinity interactions (<100 μM KD) and lower-affinity interactions when Bmax was constrained, but an increased CV for low-affinity interaction when Bmax was fitted (Figure 1F). Therefore, the standard method has lower precision for low-affinity interactions as a result of over-fitting.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on analysis of coefficient of variance shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Lowering the affinity gradually reduced the T cell response without a sharp affinity threshold.
source: Using surface CD69 as a marker for T cell activation, we found that lowering the affinity gradually reduced the response without the sharp affinity threshold suggested by near-perfect discrimination and, remarkably, responses were seen to ultra-low-affinity peptides, such as NYE 5F (KD = 1309 μM; see Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Responses were seen to ultra-low-affinity peptides, such as NYE 5F (KD = 1309 μM).
source: Using surface CD69 as a marker for T cell activation, we found that lowering the affinity gradually reduced the response without the sharp affinity threshold suggested by near-perfect discrimination and, remarkably, responses were seen to ultra-low-affinity peptides, such as NYE 5F (KD = 1309 μM; see Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Potency produced excellent correlations with KD.
source: We defined pMHC potency as the concentration of peptide required to reach 15% activation (P15) in order to include lower-affinity pMHCs and found that it produced excellent correlations with KD (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Enhanced discrimination powers (1.8–2.1) were observed that were similar for naïve, memory, and blasted T cells and for both the 1G4 and A6 TCRs.
source: We observed enhanced discrimination powers (1.8–2.1) that were similar for naïve, memory, and blasted T cells and for both the 1G4 and A6 TCRs (Figure 2K), and when using IL-2 as a measure of T cell activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2K.

claim: Large ∼1000-fold variation in antigen sensitivity was observed despite similar discrimination powers.
source: Despite these similar discrimination powers, we observed large ∼1000-fold variation in antigen sensitivity (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Similar large values of α (12, 18, and >5.1) were found for OT-I when using functional data from other studies.
source: We found similar large values of α (12, 18, and >5.1) for OT-I when using functional data from other studies (Alam et al., 1996; Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Figure 3—source data 1 ID 1–4).
evidence: This is a result from re-analysis of published data.

claim: Revised SPR data for OT-I revealed no binding for the E1 peptide variant.
source: Revised SPR data for OT-I revealed no binding for the E1 peptide variant (Stepanek et al., 2014), and therefore, we could not use the original potency data.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stepanek et al., 2014.

claim: Combining measurements of antigen potency and binding for four peptides produced an appreciably lower discrimination power of 2.1 for OT-I.
source: To produce an estimate of α for OT-I, we combined measurements of antigen potency (Daniels et al., 2006) and binding (Stepanek et al., 2014) that were now available for four peptides and found an appreciably lower discrimination power of 2.1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a result from re-analysis of published data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Revised SPR data for the 3.L2 TCR showed a wider variation in KD than originally reported.
source: In the case of the 3.L2 TCR, revised SPR data for the original four peptide variants showed a wider variation in KD than originally reported (Hong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hong et al., 2015.

claim: Re-plotting the 2B4 TCR potency data over revised binding data produced a lower discrimination power of 2.8.
source: Similarly, re-plotting the 2B4 TCR potency data over revised binding data (Wu et al., 2002) produced a lower discrimination power of 2.8 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a result from re-analysis of published data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Analysis of other mouse and human TCRs produced discrimination powers that were significantly lower than those produced using the original mouse TCR data.
source: Strikingly, analysis of these TCRs, and other mouse and human TCRs (Figure 3J), produced discrimination powers that were also significantly lower than those produced using the original mouse TCR data (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a result from analysis of published data shown in Figure 3I and 3J.

claim: No significant differences were found between CD4+ or CD8+ T cells in discrimination power.
source: We next investigated factors that might affect the TCR discriminatory power. Using the literature data, we found no significant differences between CD4+ or CD8+ T cells (Figure 3K) or across different T cell responses (Figure 3L), which is consistent with a TCR proximal mechanism for discrimination.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of published data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: No significant differences were found across different T cell responses in discrimination power.
source: We next investigated factors that might affect the TCR discriminatory power. Using the literature data, we found no significant differences between CD4+ or CD8+ T cells (Figure 3K) or across different T cell responses (Figure 3L), which is consistent with a TCR proximal mechanism for discrimination.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of published data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The lack of differences between CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and across different T cell responses is consistent with a TCR proximal mechanism for discrimination.
source: We next investigated factors that might affect the TCR discriminatory power. Using the literature data, we found no significant differences between CD4+ or CD8+ T cells (Figure 3K) or across different T cell responses (Figure 3L), which is consistent with a TCR proximal mechanism for discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of differences observed.

claim: When CD4/CD8 co-receptor binding was abolished, there was a significant increase in the discrimination power.
source: When we analysed studies where CD4/CD8 co-receptor binding was abolished (Lo et al., 2019; Laugel et al., 2007; Burrows et al., 2010), we found a significant increase in the discrimination power (Figure 3M and N), suggesting that the well-established role of co-receptors in increasing T cell sensitivity to antigen is accompanied by a decrease in discriminatory power.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of published data shown in Figure 3M and N.

claim: The well-established role of co-receptors in increasing T cell sensitivity to antigen is accompanied by a decrease in discriminatory power.
source: When we analysed studies where CD4/CD8 co-receptor binding was abolished (Lo et al., 2019; Laugel et al., 2007; Burrows et al., 2010), we found a significant increase in the discrimination power (Figure 3M and N), suggesting that the well-established role of co-receptors in increasing T cell sensitivity to antigen is accompanied by a decrease in discriminatory power.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that discrimination power increases when co-receptors are abolished.

claim: α decreased significantly from 2.0 on APCs to 0.93 on artificial surfaces where antigen was presented in isolation.
source: We also identified studies where the antigen was presented on artificial surfaces in isolation (e.g. recombinant pMHC immobilised on plates; Aleksic et al., 2010; Dushek et al., 2011; Lever et al., 2016; Abu-Shah et al., 2020) and found that α decreased significantly from 2.0 on APCs to 0.93 on these surfaces (Figure 3O).
evidence: This is a result from analysis of published data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: The discrimination power decreased from 2.0 when antigen was presented on APCs to 1.1 when presented as recombinant pMHC on plates for 1G4 T cell blasts.
source: Using our 1G4 T cell blasts, we confirmed that the discrimination power decreased from 2.0 when antigen was presented on APCs to 1.1 when presented as recombinant pMHC on plates (Figure 4A,B,D,F).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4.

claim: Other factors, beyond TCR/pMHC, may be required for enhanced discrimination.
source: This suggested that other factors, beyond TCR/pMHC, may be required for enhanced discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that discrimination is lower on plates than on APCs.

claim: Co-signalling receptors CD2 and LFA-1 may be factors required for enhanced discrimination because of their role in increasing ligand potency.
source: We hypothesised that co-signalling receptors CD2 and LFA-1 may be such factors because of their role in increasing ligand potency (Bachmann et al., 1997; Bachmann et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known roles of CD2 and LFA-1 supported by citations.

claim: Addition of recombinant ICAM1 or CD58 increased TCR downregulation and antigen potency.
source: Indeed, addition of recombinant ICAM1 (a ligand of LFA-1) or CD58 (the ligand to CD2) increased TCR downregulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and antigen potency (Figure 4C) in this experimental system, consistent with previous reports using APCs (Bachmann et al., 1997; Bachmann et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 164-fold variation in KD was amplified into a >1,600-fold variation in potency when CD58 or ICAM1 were added.
source: The potency plots highlighted that the 164-fold variation in KD was now amplified into a >1,600-fold variation in potency (Figure 4E) compared to only 414-fold when antigen was presented in isolation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The discrimination power increased from 1.1 to >1.5 when CD58 or ICAM1 were added.
source: This is reflected in the discrimination power, which increased from 1.1 to >1.5 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Engagement of the co-signalling receptors CD2 and LFA-1 enhances not only antigen sensitivity but also discrimination.
source: Therefore, engagement of the co-signalling receptors CD2 and LFA-1 enhances not only antigen sensitivity but also discrimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental results showing increased discrimination and sensitivity with CD2 and LFA-1 engagement.

claim: There are no estimates for the number of steps and the time delay in the kinetic proofreading model for T cells discriminating antigens using APCs.
source: Despite being introduced more than 20 years ago (McKeithan, 1995) and underlying all models of T cell activation (Lever et al., 2014), there are no estimates for two crucial parameters in the model, namely the number of steps and the time delay for T cells discriminating antigens using APCs.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: An unexpectedly small number of biochemical steps (2.67) was found when fitting the APC data.
source: We found an unexpectedly small number of biochemical steps when fitting the APC data (2.67) and a similar value when independently fitting the plate data (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a result from model fitting shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The fitted kp values were similar within the APC experiments but generally smaller than the plate experiments.
source: The fitted kp values were similar within the APC experiments but generally smaller than the plate experiments (Figure 5D), and because a similar number of steps was observed in both, this translated to the time delay which was longer on APCs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a result from model fitting shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The higher discrimination power observed on APCs compared to the plate is a result of a longer time delay produced not by more steps but rather a slower rate for each step.
source: Therefore, the higher discrimination power observed on APCs compared to the plate (Figure 4F) is a result of a longer time delay produced not by more steps but rather a slower rate for each step.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model fitting results.

claim: The KP mechanism could not simultaneously achieve sensitivity and near-perfect discrimination.
source: As in previous reports, we found that the KP mechanism could not simultaneously achieve sensitivity and near-perfect discrimination (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a result from theoretical analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The KP mechanism readily achieved sensitivity and the revised imperfect discrimination.
source: However, it readily achieved sensitivity and the revised imperfect discrimination that we now report, and interestingly, the 2.67 steps that we determined appear to be near the minimum number required to achieve this (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a result from theoretical analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The 2.67 steps appear to be near the minimum number required to achieve sensitivity and imperfect discrimination.
source: However, it readily achieved sensitivity and the revised imperfect discrimination that we now report, and interestingly, the 2.67 steps that we determined appear to be near the minimum number required to achieve this (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is an observation from theoretical analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The small number of steps may reflect the importance of maintaining a very short time delay so that antigen recognition can proceed rapidly allowing individual T cells to rapidly scan many APCs.
source: This may reflect the importance of maintaining a very short time delay so that antigen recognition can proceed rapidly allowing individual T cells to rapidly scan many APCs (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Dushek and Dushek and van der Merwe, 2014; Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The discrimination powers of cytokine receptors, RTKs, GPCRs, and CARs were all at or below 1.
source: We found that the discrimination powers of cytokine receptors, RTKs, GPCRs, and CARs were all at or below 1, and as a group, their discrimination powers were significantly lower than the TCR (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a result from analysis of published data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The discrimination powers of cytokine receptors, RTKs, GPCRs, and CARs as a group were significantly lower than the TCR.
source: We found that the discrimination powers of cytokine receptors, RTKs, GPCRs, and CARs were all at or below 1, and as a group, their discrimination powers were significantly lower than the TCR (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a result from analysis of published data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: A preliminary discrimination power of 1.3 was found for the BCR, which is intermediate between the TCR and other receptors.
source: We identified only a single study for the BCR that could be used to compute α and report a preliminary discrimination power of 1.3, which is intermediate between the TCR and other receptors.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of published data.

claim: The TCR appears to be unique in its enhanced ligand discriminatory powers.
source: Therefore, the TCR appears to be unique in its enhanced ligand discriminatory powers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of TCR discrimination to other receptors.

claim: The time delay of 2.8 s is at the shorter end of the value estimated using pMHC tetramers (8 s with 95% CI: 3–19 s).
source: This time delay is at the shorter end of the value estimated using pMHC tetramers (8 s with 95% CI: 3–19 s) (Yousefi et al., 2019) and consistent with the 4 s time delay between pMHC binding and LAT phosphorylation (Huse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison to published estimates supported by citations.

claim: The time delay of 2.8 s is consistent with the 4 s time delay between pMHC binding and LAT phosphorylation.
source: This time delay is at the shorter end of the value estimated using pMHC tetramers (8 s with 95% CI: 3–19 s) (Yousefi et al., 2019) and consistent with the 4 s time delay between pMHC binding and LAT phosphorylation (Huse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison to published measurements supported by citation.

claim: The small number of steps is reasonable because, although the TCR complex undergoes a large number of biochemical modifications, only those that must be sequential contribute.
source: The small number of steps is reasonable because, although the TCR complex undergoes a large number of biochemical modifications (Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014), only those that must be sequential contribute.
evidence: This is an explanation for the small number of steps supported by citation.

claim: Multiple ITAMs acting in parallel would not extend the proofreading chain.
source: It follows that multiple ITAMs acting in parallel would not extend the proofreading chain.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the statement that only sequential modifications contribute.

claim: The fractional number of steps (2.67) may suggest that at least one intermediate proofreading step is not instantly reversible.
source: The finding that the number of KP steps is fractional (2.67) may suggest that at least one intermediate proofreading step is not instantly reversible.
evidence: This is speculation based on the fractional number of steps.

claim: The fractional number of steps suggests that one (or more) KP step may be sustained upon pMHC unbinding.
source: Therefore, the fractional number of steps that we have observed suggests that one (or more) KP step may be sustained upon pMHC unbinding, which may represent the time delay between pMHC unbinding and the dephosphorylation of the TCR signalling complex and/or the unbinding of ZAP70 (Wang et al., 2010; Goyette et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to published studies.

claim: One distinct feature of the TCR is that recognition occurs at a cell-cell interface and is assisted by co-signalling receptors such as CD2 and LFA-1.
source: One distinct feature of the TCR is that recognition occurs at a cell-cell interface and is assisted by co-signalling receptors such as CD2 and LFA-1, which appear to be required for enhanced discrimination.
evidence: This is a known feature of TCR biology.

claim: Co-signalling receptors such as CD2 and LFA-1 appear to be required for enhanced discrimination.
source: One distinct feature of the TCR is that recognition occurs at a cell-cell interface and is assisted by co-signalling receptors such as CD2 and LFA-1, which appear to be required for enhanced discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental results showing that discrimination is lower without these receptors.

claim: The preliminary observation that the BCR may also exhibit enhanced discrimination suggests a role for ITAM-based signalling in enhanced discrimination.
source: Our preliminary observation that the BCR may also exhibit enhanced discrimination suggests a role for ITAM-based signalling in enhanced discrimination.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that BCR has enhanced discrimination.

claim: The finding that ITAM-based CARs did not exhibit enhanced discrimination argues against a role for ITAM-based signalling in enhanced discrimination.
source: While our finding that ITAM-based CARs did not exhibit enhanced discrimination argues against this, CARs are artificial chimeric molecules with defects in ITAM signalling (Gudipati et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an observation that contradicts the speculation about ITAM-based signalling, with a citation explaining potential reasons.

claim: Ligand potency usually correlates with solution or three-dimensional (3D) affinity measured by SPR.
source: Although ligand potency usually correlates with solution or three-dimensional (3D) affinity measured by SPR, there are occasional exceptions.
evidence: This is a general observation about the relationship between potency and affinity.

claim: A structural explanation was provided for a pMHC that could bind the TCR but could not activate T cells; it exhibited an unusual docking geometry that prevented co-receptor binding.
source: In one example, a structural explanation was provided for a pMHC that could bind the TCR but could not activate T cells; it exhibited an unusual docking geometry that prevented co-receptor binding (Adams et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Adams et al., 2011.

claim: It was suggested that mechanical forces could affect the TCR binding affinity to different ligands in a different way.
source: In another example, it was suggested that mechanical forces could affect the TCR binding affinity to different ligands in a different way (Liu et al., 2014; Sibener et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: It was shown that the surface or two-dimensional (2D) TCR/pMHC binding parameters measured within the T cell contact interface predicted the T cell response more accurately compared to the 3D binding parameters measured in SPR.
source: Finally, in a third example, it was shown that the surface or two-dimensional (2D) TCR/pMHC binding parameters measured within the T cell contact interface predicted the T cell response more accurately compared to the 3D binding parameters measured in SPR (Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2010.

claim: A subsequent study found that the 2D and 3D binding parameters for the 1E6 TCR were equally accurate at predicting the T cell response.
source: A subsequent study found that the 2D and 3D binding parameters for the 1E6 TCR were equally accurate at predicting the T cell response (Cole et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cole et al., 2016.

claim: There are likely to be occasional exceptions where 3D binding properties do not correlate with potency.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest that there are likely to be occasional exceptions where 3D binding properties do not correlate with potency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the examples of exceptions discussed.

claim: The basic KP mechanism was sufficient to accurately capture antigen discrimination within the physiological affinity range and when antigens are presented in the context of self pMHCs on autologous APCs.
source: We found that the basic KP mechanism was sufficient to accurately capture antigen discrimination within the physiological affinity range and when antigens are presented in the context of self pMHCs on autologous APCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on model fitting to experimental data.

claim: The basic KP mechanism alone cannot explain the phenomena of antagonism or optimal affinity.
source: However, it is known that the basic KP mechanism alone cannot explain the phenomena of antagonism or optimal affinity.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Antagonism can be explained by augmenting the KP mechanism with feedbacks.
source: Antagonism is a phenomena where lower-affinity pMHCs, which do not induce T cell responses on their own, are able to inhibit T cell activation by agonist pMHCs (Ma et al., 1999; Yang and Grey, 2003; Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Stone et al., 2011). This can be explained by augmenting the KP mechanism with feedbacks (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Francois et al., 2013; Lever et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: T cell responses eventually decreased as the affinity increased in studies that used supra-physiological TCR/pMHC affinities.
source: In studies that used supra-physiological TCR/pMHC affinities, it was observed that T cell responses eventually decreased as the affinity increased (Kalergis et al., 2001; Corse et al., 2010; Irving et al., 2012; Lever et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Optimal pMHC affinity can be explained by augmenting the KP mechanism with limited signalling.
source: This optimal pMHC affinity can be explained by augmenting the KP mechanism with limited signalling (Lever et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lever et al., 2014.

claim: The discriminatory power (α) can quantify discrimination, independently from antigen sensitivity, from experimental studies.
source: To study discrimination, we have introduced the discriminatory power (α) because it can quantify discrimination, independently from antigen sensitivity, from experimental studies.
evidence: This is a methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The term specificity has been used to refer to the discriminatory concept.
source: Previously, the term specificity has been used to refer to this discriminatory concept (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Francois et al., 2013; Dushek and Dushek and van der Merwe, 2014; Ganti et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Specificity is also commonly used to mean the opposite of promiscuity (i.e. the ability of T cells to respond to many different peptides).
source: However, specificity is also commonly used to mean the opposite of promiscuity (i.e. the ability of T cells to respond to many different peptides).
evidence: This is a statement about terminology usage in the field.

claim: Specificity and promiscuity should be used to refer to the tolerance of peptide sequence diversity while discrimination should be used to refer to the tolerance of changes in TCR/pMHC binding parameters.
source: To avoid ambiguity, we suggest that specificity and promiscuity are used to refer to the tolerance of peptide sequence diversity while discrimination is used to refer to the tolerance of changes in TCR/pMHC binding parameters.
evidence: This is a proposal for terminology to avoid ambiguity.

claim: Co-receptors decrease the discriminatory power of the TCR.
source: Using this terminology, our analysis suggests that co-receptors decrease the discriminatory power of the TCR (Figure 3M and N) and published data has demonstrated that co-receptors can increase the promiscuity of the TCR (Wooldridge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on analysis of data shown in Figure 3M and N.

claim: Co-receptors can increase the promiscuity of the TCR.
source: Using this terminology, our analysis suggests that co-receptors decrease the discriminatory power of the TCR (Figure 3M and N) and published data has demonstrated that co-receptors can increase the promiscuity of the TCR (Wooldridge et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wooldridge et al., 2010.

claim: Under the assumption of near-perfect TCR discrimination, T cell-mediated autoimmunity is often viewed as a defect in thymic-negative selection and/or peripheral tolerance mechanisms.
source: Under the assumption of near-perfect TCR discrimination, T cell-mediated autoimmunity is often viewed as a defect in thymic-negative selection and/or peripheral tolerance mechanisms (Yin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yin et al., 2012.

claim: T cell autoimmunity can arise by inappropriate increases in expression of self antigens.
source: This suggests that T cell autoimmunity can arise by inappropriate increases in expression of self antigens, and such increases have recently been implicated in T cell-mediated autoimmunity (Korem Kohanim et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Increases in self antigen expression have recently been implicated in T cell-mediated autoimmunity.
source: This suggests that T cell autoimmunity can arise by inappropriate increases in expression of self antigens, and such increases have recently been implicated in T cell-mediated autoimmunity (Korem Kohanim et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The therapeutic use of T cells in eliminating tumour cells is often limited by toxicities to lower-affinity off-tumour antigens.
source: T cells also have important roles in eliminating tumour cells but their therapeutic use is often limited by toxicities to lower-affinity off-tumour antigens (e.g. Cameron et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cameron et al., 2013.

claim: The factors identified that control antigen discrimination may enable the engineering of T cells with improved discriminatory powers that selectively reduce responses to lower-affinity off-tumour antigens.
source: The factors we have identified that control antigen discrimination, together with the proposed mechanisms that can generate near-perfect discrimination (Chan et al., 2003; Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Francois et al., 2013; Dushek and van der Merwe, 2014; Ganti et al., 2020), may enable the engineering of T cells with improved discriminatory powers that selectively reduce responses to lower-affinity off-tumour antigens.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications supported by citations.
